title: GPS clocks gain 38 microseconds a day

yt.title: GPS clocks run {c_us} microseconds fast every day #Shorts
yt.description:
Weak-field approximations: gravitational term GM/c^2 x (1/R_earth - 1/r_orbit), velocity term v^2/(2c^2), with GM = 3.986004418e14 m^3/s^2 (WGS 84), mean Earth radius 6,371 km, GPS orbit radius about 26,560 km, c = 299,792,458 m/s. Per day: +{c_gr} - {c_sr} = {c_us} microseconds. Light covers about {c_km} km in that time. GPS satellite clocks are set to a slightly lower frequency before launch to compensate (N. Ashby, "Relativity in the Global Positioning System", Living Reviews in Relativity, 2003).
Narration is AI-generated.

scenes.narration: The clocks on GPS satellites do not tick at the same rate as clocks on the ground.
Up there, gravity is weaker, so their clocks run faster, by about {c_gr_say} microseconds a day. But they also move fast, which slows them by about {c_sr_say}.

scenes.label: gained per day by a GPS clock
scenes.narration: Net, each satellite clock gains about {c_us_say} microseconds every day. We computed it from Einstein's formulas.
In that time, light travels about {c_km_say} kilometers. Left uncorrected, positions would drift by kilometers every day, so engineers tune the satellite clocks before launch.
